meta.title: What the Neighbor's Field Showed
meta.skill_frame: Author's craft: read how the writer piles one crop after another into a single run.

reader.who: Older students who read at about a fourth-grade level.
reader.why_this_level: Measured part_1 102w at FK 6.2, part_2 103w at FK 6.5, part_3 108w at FK 6.4, with mean sentences of 17 to 18 words. The load is a run of crops with no connecting words, which the reader has to hold as one picture.
reader.tone: Adult subject. Plain sentences. The lesson must not make the reader feel small.

source.basis: Adapted from Edmund Morris, Ten Acres Enough (1864), chapters I and IV, under DESIGN_RULES 2.5.
source.attribution: Edmund Morris. Ten Acres Enough: A Practical Experience. 1864. Project Gutenberg eBook #48753, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/48753, accessed 2026-11-12. Public domain in the United States.
source.adaptation: The authoring pass split long sentences, dropped rare words and simplified technical terms; no facts added.
source.survey: The small-fruit chapters of Ten Acres Enough: the poor eleven acres, the well-planted farm across the road, the planting of the strawberry rows, and the argument about a glutted market.
source.avoided: No invented details or prices beyond the ones Morris gives. The later profit tables are left out to keep the passage on one move.
source.drafted_by: LessonBot-adjacent, adapted from the named human source

session.difficulty_basis: a run of crops piled up without connecting words

script_overrides.near_copy_2: Say it in your own words. One sentence is enough.

passage.part_1: The eleven acres I bought looked poor, but the field across the road told me what they could become. That ground was matted with strawberries, and rows of strong raspberries held up their canes along the fence. A fine peach orchard stood on the same farm, ready to put out blossom in another month or two. Weeds grew there as well, more thickly than watermelons grow in New Jersey. If the neighbor's soil could carry all of that, then mine could carry it just as well. I walked the line of my new field and counted what I would put into it.
passage.part_2: I began with the small fruits, because the city market wanted them and paid for them early in the season. I laid out rows between the young peach trees, three feet apart, and set the strawberry plants one foot apart in the rows. That came to about ten thousand plants to the acre. I bought sixty thousand plants at two dollars a thousand, which was below the market price for that year. My friends told me that the market would soon be glutted with berries. Then they admitted that in the whole season they had never been able to afford enough to eat.
passage.part_3: A glutted market means more fruit than there are buyers, and my friends had described the opposite. They wanted berries and could not get them at any price they could afford. I took that as the answer to their warning about the market. A small farm near a city does not need to grow everything that a large farm grows. It needs to grow what the people of that city want and cannot easily find, and my acres lay close to the city that wanted them. That was the crop I chose for my first spring on the place, and I have never had reason to regret it.

items.prompt: What did the writer see growing on the farm across the road?

tutor_only.confirm: Strawberries, raspberries, a peach orchard, and weeds.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The opening of the passage names 'strawberries', 'strong raspberries', 'a fine peach orchard' and weeds on the neighbor's farm.
tutor_only.tell: Across the road he saw strawberries, raspberries, a peach orchard and weeds.
help: The opening of the passage lists what was growing there.
There are four things named in that list.
tutor_only.core_idea: He saw strawberries, raspberries, a peach orchard and weeds on the farm across the road.
accept_ideas: strawberries, raspberries, a peach orchard and weeds
berries, canes and a peach orchard
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

partial.ask: What else stood on that farm besides the strawberries?

if_they_say.when: They say the field across the road was empty.
if_they_say.ask: What was growing on it, according to the writer?

items.prompt: Where did the writer set his strawberry plants, and how far apart?

tutor_only.confirm: In rows between the young peach trees, with the plants one foot apart.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The sentence says he 'laid out rows between the young peach trees' and 'set the strawberry plants one foot apart in the rows'.
tutor_only.tell: He set them in rows between the young peach trees, one foot apart.
help: The sentence about the rows gives the place and the distance.
Three feet is the space between rows; one foot is the space between plants.
tutor_only.core_idea: He set them in rows between the young peach trees, with the plants one foot apart in the rows.
accept_ideas: in rows between the young peach trees, one foot apart
in rows between the peach trees, a foot apart
between the peach trees, one foot apart in the rows
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

partial.when: They say the plants went three feet apart.
partial.ask: Three feet is the space between rows. How far apart were the plants?

if_they_say.when: They say he planted them in the open field with no trees.
if_they_say.ask: What did he plant the rows between?

items.prompt: His friends warned that the market would be glutted, then said they could never afford enough berries. What does that tell us about their warning?

tutor_only.confirm: Their warning did not fit what they said next, because they wanted more berries than they could get.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The passage sets 'the market would soon be glutted' against their admission that they could never afford enough berries to eat.
tutor_only.tell: They wanted more berries than they could get, so their warning about a full market did not fit.
help: A glutted market means more fruit than buyers.
What did the friends say about their own supply of berries?
tutor_only.core_idea: The warning contradicted their own answer, since they wanted more berries than they could buy.
accept_ideas: their warning did not fit what they said next
they wanted more berries than they could get, so the market was not full
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

partial.when: They say the friends were right and the market was full.
partial.ask: If the market were full, why could the friends not get enough?

if_they_say.when: They say the writer ignored his friends because he did not like them.
if_they_say.ask: What did the friends say that went against their own warning?

items.prompt: The crops come one after another with nothing between them. What does that run make the neighbor's land sound like?

tutor_only.confirm: It makes the neighbor's land sound packed with one good thing after another.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The list runs strawberries, raspberries, a peach orchard and weeds with no pause, so the reader sees a field full of produce before the writer claims his own soil can match it.
tutor_only.tell: The crops come one after another, so the land sounds packed and the poor field looks able to produce.
help: Several crops pass before the writer says anything about his own field.
Each crop is named and the next one starts at once.
tutor_only.core_idea: It makes the land sound packed with good things.
accept_ideas: it makes the land sound packed with good things
it shows the soil can carry crop after crop
it piles up the produce so the land sounds rich
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

partial.when: They say the list shows the neighbor was a careless farmer.
partial.ask: Why does the writer put the list before he speaks about his own poor acres?

if_they_say.when: They say the list is only a list of what the writer likes to eat.
if_they_say.ask: Why does the writer put the list before he speaks about his own poor acres?

not_required: how many acres the neighbor had
tutor_only.full_idea: The run of crops makes the neighbor's land sound packed with good things, so the poor field looks able to produce.

items.prompt: Why did the writer choose small fruits for a small farm near a city?

tutor_only.confirm: Berries are wanted, sell early, and spoil quickly, so they must be sold close to home.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The last part says a small farm 'needs to grow what people want and cannot easily find', and that berries 'spoil quickly, so they travel badly and sell close to home'.
tutor_only.tell: Berries were wanted, sold early, and spoiled too quickly to travel far, so they suited a farm near a city.
help: The last part gives two reasons: what buyers want, and how the fruit travels.
A crop that spoils fast cannot be shipped far.
tutor_only.core_idea: They are wanted and sell close to home because they spoil quickly.
accept_ideas: they are wanted and sell close to home because they spoil quickly
city buyers wanted them and they could not travel far
they sold early and had to be sold nearby
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

partial.when: They say he chose berries because they were the cheapest crop to plant.
partial.ask: The passage gives reasons about buyers and travel. What are they?

if_they_say.when: They say he chose berries because his friends told him to.
if_they_say.ask: His friends warned him against berries. Why did he plant them?
